claims.title: Reversing a junction reverses its flux
claims.statement: Exchanging the concentrations at the two ends of a constant-field junction and reversing the voltage difference negates the signed flux.
assumptions: The ion, temperature, area, permeability and opening are the same in both orientations. Voltage is sender potential minus receiver potential, scaled by zF/(RT).
The proof treats both the analytic Bernoulli factor and the engine’s near-zero series in real arithmetic. A floating-point error bound for the series remains open.

numerical.result: The CPU surface tests exercised reversed routes, multiple patches and padding against the independent flux reference.

biology.observable: Signed transfer rate of the same ion in a cell pair with the endpoint conditions exchanged.
biology.finding: A single Cx43 channel carried about −5 pA at −50 mV and +4.8 to +4.95 pA at +50 mV in symmetric salt. This checks reversal of electrical current. Reversal of one ion’s flux under exchanged concentrations remains open. [Wang and Veenstra, Fig. 1](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9101407/)

claims.title: At equal voltage, junction flux follows the concentration gradient
claims.statement: At equal potentials the signed flux is scale × (sender concentration − receiver concentration). A positive scale gives flow from higher to lower concentration.
assumptions: The transport factor has value one at zero voltage. The scale is area × permeability × opening divided by mol/fmol. The direction claim requires a positive scale.

numerical.result: The equal-voltage CPU fixture exercised concentration differences of both signs and compared the signed flux with an independent scalar calculation.

biology.observable: Ion transfer across a junction at equal potentials and a measured concentration difference.
biology.finding: Near zero junction voltage, a charged tracer moved from the loaded cell to its neighbor. A separate study estimated 226 ± 75 calcein molecules/s per Cx26 channel at a 125 μM gradient, with only the donor voltage-clamped during transfer. [Palacios-Prado and Bukauskas, Fig. 2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2736430/) · [Zonta et al., Fig. 1A–C](https://doi.org/10.1186/1478-811X-11-15)

claims.title: A blocked junction carries zero flux
claims.statement: Setting the effective transport scale to zero gives zero junction flux at every voltage and concentration difference.
assumptions: The constant-field route multiplies the concentration-dependent term by its effective area, permeability and opening scale.

numerical.result: The surface blocking and equilibrium tests passed on CPU.

biology.observable: Ion transfer rate attributable to a junction under a specified blocking condition, with the assay detection limit.
biology.finding: Heptanol suppressed junctional current in a bovine epithelial cell pair, and the current returned after washout. The trace has no reported detection threshold for residual ion flux. [Wang et al., Fig. 2E–F](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20089928/)

claims.title: Two independent junction gates constrain the decay amplitudes
claims.statement: At fixed voltage, multiplying two independent relaxing gate factors gives a plateau P and terms at the fast rate, the slow rate and their sum. Their signed amplitudes satisfy P × A_mixed = A_fast × A_slow. With a nonzero plateau, measuring the fast and slow amplitudes determines the mixed amplitude.
assumptions: Each gate relaxes exponentially toward its own fixed plateau. Junction conductance is proportional to the product of the two factors with a common time origin.

The reported conductance can be divided by a common reference. Any additive background has been removed. Interpreting the three amplitudes separately requires distinct positive gate rates and a trace that resolves them.

numerical.result: Across four gate-kind pairings, five clamp voltages and six times, the compiled conductance and two route factors agreed with the independent calculation within 2.23 × 10⁻¹⁶. All 11 engine tests passed after registration, including the two-cell ionic trajectory and the comparison to one gate with the second pinned open. The tissue host admits the law for development runs.

biology.observable: Plateau and amplitudes at the fast, slow and summed rates in the same wild-type Cx43 conductance trace at a fixed voltage.
biology.finding: In wild-type rat Cx43 oocyte pairs, a −100 mV step gave fast and slow fitted time constants of 417 ± 175 ms and 7.06 ± 1.28 s, with a fast-to-slow amplitude ratio of 3. Figure 3 shows the voltage series for six pairs (mean ± SEM). The two-component fit leaves the mixed amplitude open. An independent untagged Cx43 series also resolved large fast and small slow amplitudes. Both studies fitted two decays, leaving the predicted mixed amplitude unmeasured. [Revilla et al., Fig. 3 and p. 1377](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0006-3495(99)76986-9)
biology.unit: conductance normalized to a common reference

evidence.locator: Figure 3A–C and Results, wild-type rat Cx43 homotypic junctions
evidence.context: Paired Xenopus oocytes. Untagged rat Cx43 on both sides. Same publication as the registered Cx43 steady-conductance fits.
evidence.uncertainty: Reported rounded ratio. The paper presents kinetic and conductance series from six pairs. No separate sampling interval for this amplitude ratio.
evidence.assessment: At −100 mV, fitted fast and slow times were 417 ± 175 ms and 7.06 ± 1.28 s. The fast-to-slow amplitude ratio was 3. The fitted model contains two decay terms.

evidence.locator: Results on current deactivation and Table 3, wt-Cx43/wt-Cx43 row
evidence.context: Homotypic untagged Cx43 in paired cells from a human cell line, dual whole-cell clamp at 22–25 °C. The fast and slow contributions are fractions of the initial decaying component.
evidence.uncertainty: Table 3 reports mean ± SEM across seven pairs. The WT fast time-constant comparison in their Fig. 5 and Table 2 reuses their 2004 series. The authors describe slow time constants as difficult to estimate.
evidence.assessment: At 110 mV the untagged pairs gave initial fast and slow fractions of 80.0 ± 3.8% and 20.0 ± 3.8%. The fitted components share a normalization. There is no separately measured term at the sum of the fast and slow rates.

pairs.assumption: For two independent Cx43 gates in series, the measured plateau times the mixed amplitude equals the product of the fast and slow amplitudes at fixed voltage.
pairs.independence: The rat Cx43 oocyte recordings and the wild-type controls in a human cell line came from independent teams. The 2011 paper identifies reused 2004 fast-rate data. Only the 2011 Table 3 amplitudes enter here.
pairs.comparison: At −100 mV the oocyte fast-to-slow fitted amplitude ratio was 3. At 110 mV the independent wild-type series reported 80 ± 3.8% fast and 20 ± 3.8% slow (SEM, seven pairs). Both fit two decays. Neither reports a third amplitude at the summed rate in the same trace, so the product identity remains untested.

replay.assessment: The two observed time constants cannot identify the third, summed-rate amplitude in a product of gates. A simultaneously resolved amplitude in the same trace is missing.

claims.title: Junction conductance relaxes toward a voltage-dependent target
claims.statement: At fixed voltage the intrinsic gate approaches its target with one exponential time constant and stays between its residual conductance fraction and one. Increasing voltage magnitude lowers the target if the residual fraction is below one. Reversing polarity preserves the trajectory from the same initial state.
assumptions: The junction has one intrinsic conductance state, the declared opening and closing rates, and a fixed threshold. Elapsed time is nonnegative and the initial conductance lies between the residual fraction and one.

The tissue applies an external availability multiplier to transport. The intrinsic gate keeps evolving during a block. The time-course identity assumes constant junction voltage throughout the interval.

numerical.result: Across 45 constant-voltage samples the compiled gate matched the independent reference within 1.12 × 10⁻¹⁶. In three tissue cell pairs the intrinsic gates continued moving during a 31.25 ms block, and tracer transfer after release matched the integrated reference within 8.68 × 10⁻¹⁸ fmol. At −80 and +80 mV the intrinsic steady target was 0.1003927 at each polarity.

biology.observable: Normalized junction conductance at each clamp polarity and the number and duration of decay components during a fixed-voltage step.
biology.finding: Seven wild-type Cx43 cell pairs gave residual conductances of 0.35 ± 0.01 and 0.33 ± 0.01 relative to the prepulse at positive and negative voltages. At −100 mV the same decay had two time constants, 70 ± 5 and 931 ± 54 ms (SEM). The Cells reference parameters give one time constant of 50.0 ms. An independent wild-type Cx43 series in N2a pairs reported fast and slow times of 0.25 ± 0.04 and 3.18 ± 0.12 s at 60 mV. The experiments leave exact transient polarity symmetry and the independent availability multiplier open. Both oocyte and N2a controls show voltage-dependent relaxation and two decay times at −100 mV. The registered single-time-constant law captures relaxation but misses the two measured phases at this voltage. [Sahu and Bera, Table 2 and Fig. S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3607587/) · [Moreno et al., Fig. 5A and Table 2](https://doi.org/10.1161/hh0402.105667)

evidence.locator: Table 1, RCx43–RCx43 row, and Fig. 3C.
evidence.context: Homotypic wild-type rat Cx43 in paired Xenopus oocytes, with conductance normalized to a 10 mV prepulse.
evidence.uncertainty: Table 1 reports rounded parameters for both fitted curves. Uncertainties for those parameters and their covariance are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: At −80 and +80 mV the published fits give 0.48745 and 0.38171. A model predicting the same value at both voltages must miss at least one fit by 0.05287 in normalized conductance (rounded). A significance test on paired observations remains open.

evidence.locator: Figure 3A–C and Results, wild-type rat Cx43 homotypic junctions
evidence.context: Paired Xenopus oocytes. Untagged rat Cx43 on both sides. Same publication as the registered Cx43 steady-conductance fits.
evidence.uncertainty: Reported rounded ratio. The paper presents kinetic and conductance series from six pairs. No separate sampling interval for this amplitude ratio.
evidence.assessment: At −100 mV, fitted fast and slow times were 417 ± 175 ms and 7.06 ± 1.28 s. The fast-to-slow amplitude ratio was 3. The fitted model contains two decay terms.

evidence.citation: Sahu and Bera (2013), Table 2 and Fig. S2
evidence.locator: Table 2, wild-type Cx43 row, Fig. S2 and Results on current decay
evidence.context: Homotypic Cx43 in N2a cell pairs, transjunctional step to −100 mV for kinetics.
evidence.uncertainty: Means ± SEM for seven pairs. These are fitted time constants in a fixed-voltage clamp.
evidence.assessment: At −100 mV, fitted fast and slow times were 70 ± 5 and 931 ± 54 ms. Steady residual conductances at positive and negative voltages were 0.35 ± 0.01 and 0.33 ± 0.01 of the prepulse. The same trace requires more than one relaxation time.

pairs.assumption: One relaxation time describes the decay of homotypic wild-type Cx43 junction current during a sustained −100 mV step.
pairs.independence: Revilla’s group recorded paired oocytes. Sahu and Bera independently recorded N2a cell pairs. Both compared homotypic wild-type Cx43 at the same voltage.
pairs.comparison: The oocyte fit gave 417 ± 175 ms and 7.06 ± 1.28 s. The N2a fit gave 70 ± 5 ms and 931 ± 54 ms. Both resolved a fast and a slow phase. The time scales differ across preparations. The measured phases constrain the existing one-state gate and motivate the separate two-gate comparison.

replay.assessment: Both preparations have two decay phases at −100 mV. A native single relaxation has only one time constant at that voltage. FR-30 addresses the two-gate use at a declared voltage. The mixed amplitude and voltage dependence are open.

claims.title: Voltage-gated channel openings stay between zero and one
claims.statement: For the six Kv1 laws, Kir2.1 and NaV1.2, both targets lie between zero and one and both time constants are positive on the declared voltage interval. An exponential tissue stage preserves the opening bounds when its two endpoint voltages differ. At a fixed voltage each gate’s deviation from its target decays exponentially. The whole-current response combines both gates.
assumptions: Voltage is inside minus outside. Both stage endpoint voltages are between −120 and +60 mV, the elapsed time is nonnegative, and both initial gates lie in [0, 1].

The proof uses the declared kinetics and the tissue’s exponential stage in real arithmetic, including the small-step series and both branches of the regularized sodium rates. A whole-current trace at fixed voltage and concentrations is proportional to the open fraction.

numerical.result: The compiled dispatcher matched independent gate targets at 25 voltages within 2.23 × 10⁻¹⁶ and time constants within 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁵ s. All 72 stage cases stayed in [0, 1]. During the tissue block all eight gate pairs continued to move.

biology.observable: Normalized whole-current activation, decay or recovery for the same isoform, temperature, holding state and voltage-step sequence.
biology.finding: Rat Kv1.1 decay at −20 mV and 25 °C was 313 ± 82 ms (SD). Cells retained 88% of its peak after 1.5 s and gave a fit of about 8 s from an equilibrated −80 mV hold. Rat Kv1.4 retained under 2% after 3.2 s at 0 mV, versus 0.57% in Cells. Four gate parameters match that paper. Human NaV1.2 rose in 0.38 ± 0.05 ms (10–90%, SEM), versus 0.296 ms in Cells. Its fitted inactivation midpoint was −63.53 ± 0.79 mV, while Cells gave half of its −120 mV reference response at −54.9 mV. [Ranjan et al., Fig. 2C](https://doi.org/10.3389/fncel.2019.00358) · [Stühmer et al., Table I and Fig. 6](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1460-2075.1989.tb08483.x) · [Begemann et al., Table 2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s10020-019-0073-6)

claims.title: Kv1.5 activation and current retention under extracellular acidification
claims.statement: With common nonzero ionic drive, the treated/control current ratio is the product of the fully open population-scale ratio and the effective-opening ratio. For a rising Boltzmann curve of fixed positive width, translating the midpoint to the right makes the treated/control activation ratio increase strictly with voltage.
assumptions: The control has positive maximal scale and opening. Both conditions share the single-open-channel drive at the test voltage, including permeant ion, temperature and concentrations.

Transferring the separately normalized peak tails in Figure 1F to the Figure 1B current assumes equal absolute maximal conductance and comparable peak openings in both protocols. Figure 1B supplies no input to the prediction.

The registered-channel sensitivity calculation moves only the activation midpoint. Inactivation, both gate time scales, channel count, permeability, ionic drive and the registered activation slope stay fixed.

numerical.result: With equal maximal scales, stored effective openings from Figure 1F gave 0.72131 for the ratios at 0 mV and −90 mV on NumPy and compiled JAX CPU. Halving the acid maximum gave 0.36066. The native channel gave a peak ratio of 1.000 under both pH labels. Applying the +11.7 mV shift to its −6.0 mV midpoint gave 0.40493. Supplying both measured midpoints with native kinetics gave 0.69537. With explicitly varied free extracellular H, native tail curves give zero pH-induced shift in two independent protocols.

biology.observable: Peak outward current remaining at 0 mV after acidification, the activation midpoint and the effect of extracellular potassium on current at strong depolarization.

evidence.locator: Figure 1F at the 0 mV prepulse and the activation midpoints in its caption. The 75 ms step in Figure 1B is held out.
evidence.context: Wild-type human Kv1.5 expressed in HEK293 cells, whole-cell at room temperature, 100 mM internal and 10 mM external K⁺. Figure 1F uses voltage-dependent prepulse durations and peak tails at −90 mV. Figure 1B compares outward currents in a pulse from −80 to 0 mV.
fit: Figure 1F peak-tail fractions at 0 mV and the two activation midpoints
evaluation: Figure 1B 0 mV step-current ratio at pH 6.8 versus 7.3
evidence.uncertainty: Figure 1B reports SEM 0.019 over eight cells. Figure 1F normalizes each condition separately and gives neither the absolute maxima nor enough information to propagate experimental uncertainty. Reading both plotted fractions within ±0.01 gives 0.703–0.740 from graph precision alone. Both assays come from one study.
evidence.assessment: The equal-maximum projection is 0.0237 below the measured fraction. The control midpoint explains why imposing the measured shift on the default Cells gate gives a smaller ratio. Quantitative pH validation needs comparable maximum conductances and matched activation kinetics.

evidence.citation: Longobardo et al. (2001), Fig. 1 and control results
evidence.locator: Figure 1 and drug-free control results
evidence.context: Wild-type human Kv1.5 in Ltk− cells, whole-cell clamp, 4 mM extracellular K, 21–23 °C. The tail voltage changed from −40 to −30 mV between pH conditions.
evidence.uncertainty: Mean ± SEM. Midpoint groups included 38 control and 27 acidic recordings. Tail voltages differed by 10 mV between conditions.
evidence.assessment: At pH 7.4 and 6.5 the midpoint was −14.2 ± 2.1 and +3.1 ± 0.7 mV. The dominant activation time constant at +60 mV also increased from 2.10 ± 0.20 to 4.23 ± 0.30 ms. Separately normalized curves leave the absolute conductance scale open.

evidence.locator: Figures 1C/D and 9B, +100 mV
evidence.context: Wild-type human Kv1.5 in HEK293. Same study as the existing 0 mV pulse and activation curves.
evidence.uncertainty: At 0 and 3 mM external K, reported errors are SEM, n = 3 each. At 10 mM the text gives a qualitative group result, n = 5.
evidence.assessment: For the same pH change and 10 mM external K as the 0 mV comparison, the current at +100 mV was essentially unchanged. At zero external K only 38.0 ± 1.5% remained. This constrains the maximal-current interpretation at strong depolarization.

evidence.locator: Figure 2 and Results, external potassium and the conductance response
evidence.context: WT human Kv1.5 in HEK293, 20–25 °C, whole-cell tails after 300-ms prepulses.
evidence.uncertainty: Reported ± as printed. Methods generally use SEM and specify SD for nonlinear least-squares outputs.
evidence.assessment: At 0, 3.5 and 140 mM extracellular K, acid/control maximum conductance was 0.19 ± 0.02, 0.56 ± 0.01 and 0.81 ± 0.12 (n = 12, 6, 6). At 3.5 mM K the activation midpoint also shifted by +7.8 mV.

evidence.locator: Fig. 2, wild-type human Kv1.5 peak outward current in RBL cells.
evidence.context: Wild-type human Kv1.5 recorded at +40 mV at two external K concentrations and two pH values.
evidence.uncertainty: Approximate ratios within each pH condition. Authors describe the normal-pH peaks as similar. No group error or sample count given for these ratios. Intracellular free K was not measured. The pipette was titrated with KOH to pH 7.2.
evidence.assessment: At pH 7.4 the peak currents at nominal zero and 4.5 mM K were similar. At pH 6.0 the zero-K current was about one tenth of the 4.5 mM value. The current example supplies an in-range test of the interaction.

biology.finding: Measured activation curves from one preparation predict its separate 0 mV pulse approximately. In the registered voltage-only gate, changing extracellular H produces zero midpoint shift. Independent experiments resolve a positive shift and potassium-dependent suppression of current. The +100 mV protocol exceeds the gate’s declared voltage range.

pairs.assumption: Extracellular acidification shifts human Kv1.5 activation toward more positive voltages.
pairs.independence: Trapani and Korn recorded HEK293 cells. Longobardo’s group independently recorded drug-free Ltk− cells.
pairs.comparison: The midpoint moved by +11.7 mV at pH 7.3→6.8 with 10 mM K, and by +17.3 mV at pH 7.4→6.5 with 4 mM K. Both support the sign. The different acid steps, cells and pulse protocols leave a common mV-per-pH coefficient unresolved.

replay.assessment: The compiled channel receives the two measured bath pH values in each preparation. The normalized midpoints shift by less than 10⁻¹² mV at 10 and 4 mM external K. The measured shifts are +11.7 and +17.3 mV. A voltage-independent availability multiplier cancels in the normalized curve.

pairs.assumption: Higher external potassium reduces the suppression of Kv1.5 current by extracellular acidification at strong depolarization.
pairs.independence: The Connecticut and British Columbia groups collected separate whole-cell recordings. Trapani’s high-voltage panels and activation curve belong to one publication.
pairs.comparison: Trapani found 38.0 ± 1.5% and 97.7 ± 0.3% of control current at +100 mV with 0 and 3 mM K (pH 7.3→6.8). Kehl found 19%, 56% and 81% of maximal conductance with 0, 3.5 and 140 mM K (pH 7.4→6.4). The direction agrees across a high-voltage current and a fitted maximum. The pH steps and readouts differ.

replay.assessment: Kehl’s fitted tail-current maximum gives a native acid/control ratio of 1 at both positive K levels. At 3.5 mM only the overlapping prepulses are admissible for the comparison. At 140 mM both full grids match. Trapani’s +100 mV step exceeds the +60 mV ceiling.

pairs.assumption: Low external potassium strengthens acid suppression of wild-type human Kv1.5.
pairs.independence: The two groups measured their own HEK293 and RBL cell preparations.
pairs.comparison: Kehl’s acid/control maximal conductance rose from 0.56 at 3.5 mM K to 0.81 at 140 mM. In Jäger’s +40 mV pulse the nominal-zero/4.5 mM peak-current ratio fell from near one at pH 7.4 to about 0.1 at pH 6.0. The ratio denominators differ. The common observation is the potassium–pH interaction.

replay.assessment: At +40 mV the near-zero/4.5 mM K peak ratio converges to 1.008 at both pH values, versus near one and about 0.1 in Jäger. Kehl’s native fitted tail maxima give acid/control ratios of 1 on the common grids, including the complete 140 mM grid. The two assays have different denominators.

claims.title: Independent channel counts determine relative availability from fixed-gate currents
claims.statement: When two populations share their single-channel drive and stored gates, the ratio of their currents per counted surface channel equals the ratio of their availabilities. Their patch areas and channel densities may differ.
assumptions: Compare the same permeant ion, voltage, charge conversion, temperature, concentrations, gate state, permeability and reference channel density. Counting uses all voltage-sensing channels, including channels that are silent.

Each patch has positive area and density. The reference preparation has positive availability and a nonzero single-channel response. The test uses the same area units for current density and channel density.

The descriptive density curve fixes the Hill exponent at one and basal fraction at zero. Its maximum and half-saturation come from the two Kv1.5 endpoints. The composite exercises a distinct reporter. D218 excludes using a population’s own density to route its own availability.

numerical.result: On three Kv1.5 patches of 100, 160 and 240 µm², the count-normalized currents relative to the low-density patch were 1, 1 and 1 at fixed availability. With the measured fractions supplied, they were 1, 0.6765 and 0.5294 at both clamp voltages on NumPy and compiled JAX CPU. The separate reporter returned 0.22215 at 300 channels/µm², matching the reciprocal interpolation.

biology.observable: Kv1.5 conducting fraction at a middle density excluded from fitting, and whether changes in the channel’s own density cause those changes in availability.

evidence.locator: Fig. 8C, journal p. 766. The orange triangle nearest 300 channels/µm² is the evaluation point.
evidence.context: Tagged Kv1.5 in HEK293 cells at room temperature. Conducting-channel estimates use ionic conductance, and voltage-sensing channel counts use calibrated gating charge. The density series compares different cells.
evidence.uncertainty: Graph readings of three-cell moving averages from one study. There are no pointwise errors. The estimated gating count occurs in the density numerator and the conducting-fraction denominator, so error in that count can induce anticorrelation.
evidence.assessment: The middle estimate is about 0.23. The two-endpoint inhibition curve gives about 0.22 there and a constant fraction calibrated at the low density gives 0.34. The comparison cannot establish the Kv1.5 silencing mechanism. Nearby Kv1.4 fractions were about 0.64 and 0.73.

claims.title: A fixed-gate current curve identifies the product of channel abundance and availability
claims.statement: At a declared voltage, the population’s outward electrical current is its outward permeant-ion flux times the signed charge per fmol. With fixed stored gates and known drive, two abundance and availability pairs give the same current at every sampled voltage exactly when their products agree, provided at least one voltage gives a nonzero response at unit abundance and availability.
assumptions: The channel conducts one declared ion. The charge, concentrations, temperature, area and permeability defining its single-population drive are known and shared across the two preparations.

The readout uses the stored gates. Abundance is proportional to surface count at fixed patch area and reference density. At reversal or with closed gates, a zero signal alone cannot determine the product.

numerical.result: On the tissue host, 11 active populations on two patches agreed with the 70-digit reference within 1.30 × 10⁻²⁶ A. Halving abundance or availability halved current exactly. Full block, off-ion fluxes and padding gave zero. On the repaired composite the public clamp reproduced the observed 0.658534 pA at the patch voltage and gave 0.296208 pA at −50 mV with availability 0.5. The raw scheduled control gave 0.592416 pA there.

biology.observable: A matched signed current at a declared voltage with independent measurements of channel abundance, the fraction available to conduct, stored gate state and unitary drive.

evidence.locator: Fig. 8B reports the group means. Fig. 8C, p. 766, orange triangles, gives the density series for Kv1.5.
evidence.context: Tagged Kv channels in HEK293 cells at room temperature. Channel estimates use gating charge, fluorescence calibration, ionic slope conductance near reversal and current fluctuations.
evidence.uncertainty: The two Kv1.5 endpoints are approximate readings of a three-cell moving average near 115 and 425 gating channels/µm². No endpoint uncertainties are given. Group means were 0.96 ± 0.05 for Kv1.4 and 0.26 ± 0.01 for Kv1.5 (SEM).
evidence.assessment: A conducting fraction held at the low-density value would predict 0.34 at the high-density endpoint, where the figure gives about 0.18. Density changes across cells. The measured fractions constrain an availability model across densities. A matched test of absolute instantaneous current remains open.

claims.title: Channel opening scales the signed transfer of sodium or potassium
claims.statement: The seven gated K⁺ laws, one gated Na⁺ law and two single-ion leaks multiply the fully open constant-field flux by their opening and external availability. The opening is m h² for Kv1.1 and Kir2.1, m h for Kv1.2–Kv1.6, m³ h for NaV1.2 and one for the two leaks. With availability between zero and one the magnitude cannot exceed the fully open flux. Blocking gives zero. Only the declared ion crosses, debiting the cell and crediting the exterior. With a block fraction determined by V − E at fixed dose, matched driving voltages give equal blocked/free current ratios wherever the free currents are nonzero.
assumptions: The declared population conducts K⁺ or Na⁺ with relative permeability one. The same area, permeability, abundance, voltage and concentrations define the fully open comparison. Positive flux points from the cell to the exterior.
The gate values and external availability are in [0, 1]. The formal booking uses one cell–exterior pair. A held bath offsets the exterior credit with reservoir supply.

numerical.result: All ten populations shared one membrane. Potassium moved out and sodium moved in after release. Every off-ion and padding transfer was zero. The largest per-channel cumulative discrepancy was 2.37 × 10⁻¹³ fmol against an independent adaptive solution.

biology.observable: Ion-specific flux or current at known driving force, with an independently measured availability or single-channel open fraction.
biology.unit: fmol/s or pA with the ion charge identified
biology.finding: At −60 mV, 100 µM cytoplasmic spermine reduced the Kir2.1 single-channel current magnitude from 2.00 ± 0.04 to 1.40 ± 0.04 pA with no significant change in open probability. A voltage-only gate misses that change in unitary conductance. The two generic leak laws have no assigned molecular isoform or preparation-specific permeability. [Xie et al., Figs. 1–3](https://doi.org/10.1085/jgp.20028576)

evidence.locator: Fig. 3A,C and Eq. 4.
evidence.context: Kir2.1 in excised HEK-cell patches at 24–26 °C, high symmetric K, intracellular spermine.
evidence.uncertainty: 4.8 mV is the fitted e-fold scale of high-affinity Kd versus voltage. The paper gives no separate uncertainty for this fit.
evidence.assessment: This corresponds to apparent valence 5.33–5.37. The local half-block slope of total current is a different observable.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 and Table 1.
evidence.context: Excised Kir2.1 patches in symmetric high K. A two-component fit was made to blocked-to-free relative current with 300 µM intracellular spermine.
evidence.uncertainty: Mean ± SEM across seven patches. The estimate depends on separating shallow and steep components.
evidence.assessment: The steep component gave an effective valence of 5.0 ± 0.2. This corresponds to 5.17 mV per e-fold at the fit temperature of 300 K.

evidence.locator: Figs. 2–3 and reversal-shift analysis.
evidence.context: Kir2.1 expressed in oocytes. Internal and external K were varied separately during polyamine block.
evidence.uncertainty: The shift ratios are fitted relationships in this preparation. Lopatin also coauthored the 2006 study.
evidence.assessment: At 20 µM spermine the shift in rectification per change in K reversal was +0.91 for external K and −0.15 for internal K. A universal V−E offset would give +1 for both. In Fig. 3C, increasing internal K from 150 to 625 mM shifts half-block by about +5 mV while the reversal shifts about −36 mV. The native FR-51 controls predict −36.3 mV or zero.

evidence.citation: Panama and Lopatin (2006), Figs. 3A,E,F and Table 2
evidence.locator: Fig. 3A and E supply approximate reversals and relative-current curves.
evidence.context: Mouse Kir2.1 in HEK293 outside-out patches, 30 µM total and about 7 µM free spermine.
evidence.uncertainty: Representative curves lack pointwise errors. The unblocked current was extrapolated and matching of the example panels to one patch is unspecified.
evidence.assessment: Half of the total normalized conductance shifted about +51.6 mV for a measured +53.2 mV reversal shift. The separate pooled steep-mode slope was 0.98 ± 0.01 across two patches.

evidence.locator: Upward triangles at 1 µM, normalized to the 0.1 µM conductance maximum.
evidence.context: Wild-type Kir2.1, HEK293T inside-out patches, 24–25 °C. Each K concentration uses different patches.
evidence.uncertainty: 150 mM n=5, 50 mM n=6–8 and 20 mM n=2. The 20 mM group has no reported errors. Graph reading is about 1 mV and 0.03 in conductance fraction near the transition.
evidence.assessment: The total half-conductance shifts were about −26.1 and −48.1 mV against measured reversal shifts −26.9 and −48.9 mV. The resulting ratios of about 0.97 and 0.98 use measured curve points and share a calibration.

pairs.assumption: A single tetravalent blocker moving through at most the full electric field can account for the steep component of Kir2.1 spermine block.
pairs.independence: The Ishihara and Panama groups recorded independent patches and used different fitting protocols. The second paper cites the first.
pairs.comparison: Two fits to excised-patch data give a steep apparent valence above four. The fitted high-affinity Kd slope gives 5.33–5.37. The fitted steep component of relative current gives 5.0 ± 0.2 (SEM, seven patches).

replay.assessment: Halving prescribed Kir2.1 availability in the native clamp gave a current ratio of 0.5 at all four voltages. The measured steep components exceed the maximum of four from spermine charge times electrical distance. The landed FR-51 declaration admits these effective valences. Their model fits leave the number of displaced ions unmeasured. [FR-51 on main](https://github.com/Eidosoma/Cells/blob/f8c6c32665c1ba8c0bcd8b687e4a7f961dc1cc5e/src/cells/laws/channels/open_channel_block.py#L7-L17)

pairs.assumption: With a fixed intracellular spermine dose in each preparation, changing external potassium moves the half-conductance voltage of Kir2.1 approximately with its measured potassium reversal.
pairs.independence: Independent laboratories recorded wild-type Kir2.1 in excised patches. The normalization, blocker dose and patch configuration differ. Each comparison uses its own preparation and calibration.
pairs.comparison: Half the total normalized conductance shifted +51.6 mV for a +53.2 mV reversal shift in Panama, and −26.1 and −48.1 mV for −26.9 and −48.9 mV shifts in Ishihara. The latter two share the 150 mM curve. Exact slope and absolute current remain unresolved.

replay.assessment: In the development @3 clamp, RMS fraction errors with measured shifts were 0.044, 0.010 and 0.015. Concentration-based reversals gave 0.226, 0.026 and 0.043. True absolute-voltage blocks gave 0.397, 0.479 and 0.533. Internal K has one separate contrary series. D391 stopped the post-landing registration under §3 because the 10 mM trace could not be identified. Both held-out levels (10 and 20 mM) remain unread and unscored. [Exploratory replay](PROGRESS.md#fr51-two-potassium) · [Registration stop](PROGRESS.md#fr51-panama-holdouts)

claims.title: Chloride gradients set leak reversal and inward chloride carries positive outward current
claims.statement: For the gate-free Cl⁻ population, outward material flux J produces outward electrical current −F × 10⁻¹⁵ × J amperes for J in fmol/s. The conducting route reverses at V = (RT/F) × (ln inside − ln outside) on the regular Bernoulli branch and at zero voltage. On the small nonzero branch its reversal follows the implemented polynomial ratio.
assumptions: Voltage is inside minus outside. Concentrations, absolute temperature, F and RT are positive. Permeability, area, abundance and availability give a positive scale for the reversal claim.

The formal calculation is over real numbers. The regular branch uses |FV/(RT)| ≥ 10⁻⁴. The sign conversion applies to either flux branch. In the tissue comparison, a single membrane connects the cell to a grounded bath and the chloride population is the only conductive route.

numerical.result: At the same initial voltage, 147 and 70 mM bath chloride gave opposite fluxes and initial electrode currents of +0.573 and −5.733 pA. The two tissue trajectories matched an independent solution within 1.58 × 10⁻¹² fmol of transfer, with zero off-ion and padding flux.

biology.observable: Shift in the single-channel reversal potential when the nominal extracellular chloride concentration changes at fixed intracellular chloride and temperature.

pairs.assumption: Lowering extracellular chloride shifts the reversal of a chloride-selective epithelial current in the positive direction.
pairs.independence: Ling and Bajnath studied different epithelial preparations in separate laboratories. Both measured single-channel currents in cell-attached patches, with voltages relative to resting potential.
pairs.comparison: Rabbit collecting-duct patches shifted about +45 mV for 145→15 mM external Cl⁻ at 37 °C (Cells +60.63). Human colon patches shifted +23 mV for 150→57 mM at 25 °C (Cells +24.86). Both support direction. The rabbit magnitude falls short of the ideal shift; endpoint errors and ion activities limit a quantitative comparison.

replay.assessment: At each assay’s temperature and outside chloride concentrations the native roots shift +60.63 and +24.86 mV. The measured shifts are about +45 and +23 mV. Activities and endpoint errors limit the rabbit magnitude comparison.

evidence.locator: Methods, Fig. 2 and accompanying Results, closed-to-open single-channel amplitudes.
evidence.context: Forskolin-stimulated, cell-attached patches of human HT-29cl.19A epithelium at 25 °C. Pipette chloride was lowered with osmotic compensation.
evidence.uncertainty: The high-chloride reversal was 2 ± 1 mV on the −Vₚ scale. The low-chloride endpoint was about 25 mV. No error on their difference was reported.
evidence.assessment: Lowering external chloride shifted the reversal positive. Cells gives +24.86 mV at 25 °C for a fixed internal chloride concentration. The inside-out control at symmetric chloride was a separate experiment.

evidence.locator: Figure 1B and accompanying Results.
evidence.context: Cell-attached apical patches of cultured rabbit collecting-tubule principal cells at 37 °C. Pipette chloride was lowered from 145 to 15 mM by partial substitution with gluconate. The voltage scale is relative to the resting membrane potential.
evidence.uncertainty: The two conditions used 11 and 4 patches, with no endpoint uncertainty reported.
evidence.assessment: The measured shift is approximate. Lowering nominal outside chloride from 145 to 15 mM in rabbit kidney patches at 37 °C shifted reversal in the predicted positive direction. The channels also passed bromide and showed regulated opening. Absolute permeability remains uncalibrated.

claims.title: Passive neutral solute follows its concentration gradient
claims.statement: For a neutral solute the inward constant-field flux is the route scale times outside minus inside concentration at any voltage. With a positive scale it is inward exactly when concentration is higher outside. In a closed pair the gradient changes at rate −k times the gradient, where k is the scale times the sum of the reciprocal compartment volumes.
assumptions: Valence is zero. The route scale is area × permeability × opening divided by mol/fmol. Concentrations are in mM and flux is in fmol/s.
The relaxation identity applies to two well-mixed compartments at fixed positive volumes in pL, with this route as the sole transfer of the solute.

numerical.result: Five compiled cases agreed with the independent flux within 7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ fmol/s. In the closed tissue pair at 20 ms, the largest relative error in final compartment amount was 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ against a 5 × 10⁻⁴ tolerance.

biology.observable: Signed passive transfer rate of an identified neutral solute at measured free concentrations on both sides, with compartment volumes or measured flux per area and the corresponding area.
biology.finding: Urea flux was measured over time in liposomes of three lipid compositions. Comparing a Cells rate requires the gradient, area and permeability for the same preparation. [Lande et al., Fig. 3](https://doi.org/10.1085/jgp.106.1.67)

claims.title: Ion charge sets permeation reversal and bounds the current–voltage slope
claims.statement: For a passive ion of either sign, the analytic flux reverses at its Nernst voltage and dissipates nonnegative heat. At fixed concentrations the electrical slope conductance stays between the lower and higher concentrations multiplied by the same positive factor. Equal concentrations give a linear current–voltage relation.
assumptions: Temperature, concentrations and compartment volumes are positive. The reversal requires nonzero ion charge and positive permeability, area and opening. The conductance bound also includes a closed route.

Conductance holds at fixed concentrations, permeability and opening. In the engine’s real-arithmetic evaluator the slope bounds exclude the two switches at |zFV/(RT)| = 0.0001. The secant bound assumes the whole voltage interval stays within one branch. The material response holds at fixed volumes and voltage.

The biological current predictions assume the same effective permeability at both voltages within each preparation. A red-cell current is inferred from net solute transfer, and a planar-bilayer current is measured under voltage clamp.

numerical.result: 360 CPU float64 component cases matched high-precision flux, heat and slope references. In two finite tissue pairs, halving the step from 64 to 128 steps reduced errors in signed transfer, heat and final voltage by factors of 4.03–4.05. Both amount ledgers matched the transferred material.

biology.observable: Electrical current at a second voltage and reversal at a known ion gradient. These experiments leave microscopic route heat unmeasured.

Each series has its own fit. Bilayer readings have about 1 nA digitization precision and no reported replicate error at these voltages.

claims.title: Voltage and free proton concentrations set the leak reversal
claims.statement: For an open route, inward flux is positive exactly when hOut exceeds hIn × B(−x)/B(x), using the engine’s selected Bernoulli factor at x = FV/(RT). The analytic law reverses at V = (RT/F) × (ln hOut − ln hIn) and releases nonnegative instantaneous heat. The engine’s real-arithmetic evaluator gives the analytic flux at x = 0 and for |x| ≥ 10⁻⁴. At other x the polynomial has its own reversal ratio. At fixed voltage and opening, the change in inward flux is scale × B(x) times the change in free outside concentration.
assumptions: Positive free H⁺ concentrations on both sides in mM, positive absolute temperature and proton valence +1. Voltage is inside minus outside, with positive flux inward.
Area × permeability × opening is positive for directional claims and may be zero for the heat inequality. The proof interprets both evaluator branches in real arithmetic.

numerical.result: Twelve compiled CPU cases agreed with the 70-digit flux reference within 1.55 × 10⁻²⁰ fmol/s. In a buffered tissue cell, using free H⁺ gave the observed inward rate of 3.31 × 10⁻⁶ fmol/s. Substituting total intracellular proton equivalents reversed the predicted direction. Eight additional composite clamps tracked lumen pH at fixed voltage when bath pH varied independently. Version 1 refused the general-binding node. [Version 2](buffered-proton-reversal.md) exercises that endpoint. Six compiled roots agreed with the Nernst values at nominal pipette and bath pH to within 10⁻¹⁰ mV. At microglial pipette/bath pH 5.5/7.8 the model gave −135.15 mV at 23 °C against an approximate −86 mV measured.

biology.observable: Reversal voltage of an open H⁺ path across measured pH gradients at known temperature. Predicting the signed flux magnitude also requires permeability, area and opening.
biology.finding: In Jurkat T cells the proton-current reversal shifted −47 mV per pH unit, versus an ideal −58 mV per pH unit. The fitted slope uncertainty and intracellular pH limit a quantitative verdict. Independent macrophage and microglia tail currents also show the sign of the pH response, with the largest departures when nominal pipette and bath pH are furthest apart. Two inner-membrane measurements share a laboratory. [Schilling et al., Fig. 2E](https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.2002.028878) Sasaki’s independent expression study also reported tail reversal near proton equilibrium. A three-lab comparison with measured pH at both membrane faces remains open. [Sasaki et al.](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1122352)

claims.title: The local free proton concentration at each buffered endpoint sets leak reversal
claims.statement: The general binding closure determines a unique free proton read at either endpoint when its equilibrium exists. At zero voltage and on the regular branch, the open leak reverses at (RT/F) times the outside-minus-inside difference in free log proton concentration. At fixed inside concentration and voltage, raising outside free H⁺ increases inward flux.
assumptions: Positive absolute temperature and route scale, valence +1, inside-minus-outside voltage and a common concentration standard. Binder totals are nonnegative. Held ligand totals and unheld free ligands agree when comparing solutions at one endpoint.
The Bernoulli evaluator agrees with the analytic reversal at zero and for |FV/(RT)| ≥ 10⁻⁴. At small nonzero voltage the earlier two-branch proof gives the evaluator’s own reversal ratio.
For the mitoplast comparison, the solution pH is used as the free-proton activity proxy. The reference temperature is the 24 °C specified for the authors’ Nernst line.

numerical.result: Across three matrix/bath pH pairs and outside buffers of 1 and 100 mM, all six clamped reversals agreed with the independent Nernst calculation within 10⁻⁶ mV. The sign changed across every root. Substituting stored total proton equivalents gave nonzero flux at each free-proton reversal.

pairs.independence: Bertholet’s group recorded mouse skeletal-muscle mitoplasts. Cherny’s group recorded rat alveolar epithelial cells with a different proton pathway.
pairs.comparison: The three mitoplast groups reversed at means of −62.2, −91.1 and +28.8 mV at outside-minus-inside pH differences of +1, +1.5 and −0.5. The alveolar tail-current reversal shifted in the same direction by about 52 mV per pH unit over four units. The shared result concerns the zero-current voltage. Permeability and gating remain separate questions.

claims.title: Free energy sets ATP-driven transport direction and stall
claims.statement: With positive forward rate J⁺, an enabled cycle has net rate J⁺(1 − exp(ΔG/RT)). It runs forward for negative ΔG, reverses for positive ΔG and stalls at zero. A disabled cycle has zero rate. Instantaneous heat is nonnegative in every case. For n protons per ATP, the stall voltage is (RT/F) ln(a_P/a_N) + ΔG_fuel/(nF). At fixed fuel, temperature and coupling, changing the pH gradient shifts stall by exactly the change in the proton equilibrium voltage. Neutral cargo flux is independent of voltage at fixed activities and forward rate.
assumptions: One tightly coupled mode hydrolyses one ATP on side N and moves n cargo units from N to P. Cargo valence is +1 for free protons and zero for the neutral role. Voltage is V_N − V_P.

Activities and absolute temperature are positive. In an enabled population, capacity, availability and the saturation factor are positive. Lean represents their product by its finite logarithm and uses real arithmetic.

numerical.result: Across 92 compiled tissue states, 72 ran forward, 16 reversed and four were within the stall tolerance. Cycle flux agreed with frozen references to 7.50 × 10⁻¹⁶ fmol/s and heat was nonnegative in all cases. Offsetting the voltage by ±10 mV about proton stall reversed the rate. The same voltage perturbations preserved all three flowing neutral controls. Eight capacity and availability controls gave exactly zero flux, heat and work. For the eight yeast assay conditions, the registered proton law also bracketed 32 stall voltages. At fixed fuel the pH-induced shift was −112.40 mV for every supported coupling.

The plant nucleotide activity quotient during the ramps is missing. Neither series counts protons per ATP. claims.title: Stall voltages and net charge of the sodium–potassium and calcium pumps
claims.statement: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stalls at ψ = g_NaK − 3r_Na + 2r_K and the calcium pump at ψ = (g_Ca − r_Ca)/2. An enabled pump runs forward above its own stall voltage. Their outward charge flux in elementary-charge equivalents is J_NaK + 2J_Ca. The same sum determines their voltage-dependent free-energy change. The two currents cancel exactly when J_NaK = −2J_Ca.
assumptions: For each ion, r is ln(inside activity / outside activity), ψ = F(V_inside − V_outside)/(RT), and each g is its pump’s ATP hydrolysis free energy divided by RT. Temperature and all activities are positive. The direction and stall results assume positive capacity, availability and saturation.

J denotes signed cycles per unit time. Each forward cycle consumes one ATP. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump exports three Na⁺ and imports two K⁺. The Cells calcium pump transports one Ca²⁺ outward and counts only that ion. The formula sums the currents of these two pumps.

numerical.result: The compiled tissue matched two 80-digit references at five initial voltages, including both stalls (−99.365 and −104.104 mV). The largest cycle-rate error was 3.50 × 10⁻¹⁶ fmol/s. At the midpoint the pumps ran in opposite directions, each contributing 0.349 pA in magnitude. The net electrode current was 2.04 × 10⁻²⁶ A. The 1 ms trajectory accounted for all three ions and both midpoint pumps dissipated energy.

biology.observable: Ion transfer per ATP, paired ion flux and outward current, and stall voltage under known fuel and ion activities. A separate erythrocyte measurement reports labelled phosphate incorporation into ATP.
biology.finding: Squid axons gave 3.05 ± 0.13 Na⁺ per net charge from −60 to −90 mV in Na-free seawater and 2.72 ± 0.09 at 0 mV with 390 mM external Na⁺ (SEM). Cells predicts 3. Red-cell ghosts lost about 3 Na⁺ per ATP. In pig-brain calcium pumps, separate rate measurements imply 1.02 Ca²⁺ per ATP and about +1.4 net charges per ATP after inward H⁺ is included. Cells counts +2 from Ca²⁺ alone. The simulated stall voltages still lack a matched measurement.
