claims.title: Finite molecule counts set stochastic encounter rates and paired event heat
claims.statement: A molecular encounter draws from the available counts without replacement. For a regular, finite two-way edge with a common locus extent and catalyst factor, log(forward rate / reverse rate) equals minus the free-energy change plus held-reservoir work. At full membrane consumption the declared cancellation determines the boundary rate.
assumptions: Counts and reaction coefficients are natural numbers. The engine admits at most three reactants or products per side. The factorial identity holds for any finite integer order.

For the regular pair identity the residual membrane count after drawing all reactants is at least the measure offset. At offset one, full consumption without a shared participant uses the cancelled denominator. Overlap at full order can give a singular rate. The kept, extinct and reversible tokens govern which boundary events can fire.
The occupancy specialization uses one R molecule, distinct G partners, an ideal dilute pool and two reversible states at fixed volume.

numerical.result: The reference and engine agreed on ordinary rates and zero and singular patterns across 594 compositions under both count measures. Three boundary conventions were checked on six additional states. The pool kernel reproduced the two-state occupancy formula at one, two and three partners.

biology.observable: Bound probability for one molecule as the integer count of its distinct partner changes, and association events for identical reactants at known counts.
biology.finding: For identical membrane partners, live-cell homodimer imaging measured a 91 ± 16 ms lifetime. It reported surface densities, leaving the repeated-reactant draw at fixed small counts open. [Kasai et al., Figs. 4–6](https://doi.org/10.1083/jcb.201009128)

evidence.locator: Experimental grey bars for one dimer in the three classes with one red strand, at 250 nm radius. Table 1 and Fig. S8 provide the kinetic and independent bulk estimates.
evidence.context: Red- and green-labelled complementary strands confined in sealed dimples. Each class fixes the counts of the two distinct partners.
fit: One red molecule and one green partner
evaluation: One red molecule and two green partners
One red molecule and three green partners
evidence.uncertainty: The figure shows error bars without tabulated uncertainties for individual bars. We calibrated on the one-partner class and evaluated the other classes from the same experiment. This cancels the common chamber volume. The authors fitted their confined dissociation constant using all classes. A separate calculation using bulk Kd depends appreciably on the volume estimate.
evidence.assessment: From one partner’s measured 0.48 bound probability, Cells predicted 0.649 and 0.735 with two and three partners. The figure gives about 0.64 and 0.67, respectively.

claims.title: A common catalyst factor preserves reversible rate ratios and equilibrium weights
claims.statement: On a positive reversible edge, catalysis preserves the forward-to-reverse rate ratio exactly when both rates receive the same multiplier. The transition-state law assigns a positive factor from the molecules common to both endpoints. The same equilibrium weights then balance the edge.
assumptions: The stabilizations are finite, dimensionless contact energies in kBT. A nonempty common membrane uses its molecular fractions. An empty common membrane has factor 1.
The rate-ratio identity refers to an available two-way transition. The equilibrium statement assumes the original rates and weights obey detailed balance on each edge.

numerical.result: The directional multipliers agreed with the exact common-state value on 1,925 ordinary reversible edges. In the opposed ±20 kBT contact case, both rates were 2.0611536224/s and the first event occurred at the reference 0.3459699807 s. All four seeded clocks fired four events with closed ledgers. The earlier comparison records the spurious inert state.

biology.observable: Forward and reverse molecular transfer rates and an independently measured equilibrium partition under matched temperature and catalyst concentration.
biology.unit: s⁻¹ for each direction, dimensionless equilibrium partition
biology.finding: At 37 °C, cholesterol exchange between vesicles sped up about 57-fold with 1 mM β-cyclodextrin. Half-times were 195 ± 13 and about 3.4 minutes. A separate 0.5 mM equilibrium series gave a partition coefficient of 0.91 ± 0.06. Equal scaling of the two directional rates remains unmeasured. This transfer catalyst is in solution. [Leventis and Silvius, Figs. 1–2 and Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0006-3495(01)75873-0)

claims.title: Potassium rectification sets reversal, dissipation and a bound on slope conductance
claims.statement: On an open route the outward current changes sign at the Nernst potential and dissipates nonnegative heat. At fixed drive it scales with the square root of external concentration. The voltage derivative obeys the host’s upper bound even when the differential conductance is negative.
assumptions: The route carries a monovalent cation. Concentrations, absolute temperature, reference concentration and slope parameter are positive. The gain includes nonnegative area, availability and reference conductance. Reversal and sign require positive gain.

The derivative holds concentrations and route parameters fixed. The biological matched-drive comparison uses constant availability, rectification parameters and number of contributing channels across the potassium series.

numerical.result: All three equivalent normalizations gave 0.5520533 pA and identical transfer and heat, including the smallest normal float64 potassium reference. All 360 voltage controls passed. A positive subnormal reference (5 × 10⁻³²⁴ mM) was refused during definition checking. The original overflow remains at the earlier engine revision.

biology.observable: Kir4.1 unitary current 60 mV below reversal, inward unitary slope conductance and the shift in reversal as external potassium changes. Separately, inward unitary slope in sodium-poor mouse Kir2.1 and native ventricular recordings.

evidence.locator: Panel C gives reversal, B(b) gives unitary currents and D fits the inward slope conductances from the same patch series.
evidence.context: Cloned rat Kir4.1 in HEK293T cell-attached patches at about 25 °C, three patches per concentration.
evaluation: 15, 21, 35 and 63 mM at a common −60 mV drive
evidence.uncertainty: Currents are approximate graph readings interpolated after reading the reversal for each series. Some reversal markers overlap. Per-point numerical uncertainties are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: At 15 mM external K the current magnitude fell less than the model predicted, as it did at the other three held-out concentrations. The model’s −59.67 mV shift in reversal agreed with the approximately −60 mV measured.

evidence.locator: Figure 7B–C and adjacent Results
evidence.context: Human Kir4.1 in cell-attached Xenopus oocyte patches, pH 7.4, pipette magnesium 1 mM. Changes in pipette KCl were balanced by NaCl.
evidence.uncertainty: 10 and 40 mM are approximate figure readings. The 110 mM value is in the text. Figure errors were plotted without numerical errors or a stated sample count for each point.
evidence.assessment: At 10, 40 and 110 mM external K the inward slope was approximately 8, 19 and 23 pS. The authors fitted saturation (maximum 24.4 pS, half-maximal K 16.7 mM, exponent 1.4). Their modeled reversal offsets supply no independent reversal measurement.

evidence.locator: Figure 5B, two raw current–voltage curves in a frog Müller cell
evidence.context: Whole-cell recording from retinal glia with 100 mM intracellular K and 3 mM added intracellular spermine.
evidence.uncertainty: Approximate visual shifts within one cell. No numerical uncertainty on the crossings. Native current may include other channels.
evidence.assessment: A tenfold increase in external K moved the raw current crossing about +50 mV. The separate breakpoint for fast block moved about +100 mV. Native Müller-cell current supports the direction of reversal with a less specific channel assignment.

evidence.locator: Fig. 4B–C, wild-type mouse Kir2.1, inward unitary slope of the i–V relation.
evidence.context: Cell-attached recordings of recombinant mouse Kir2.1, with extracellular potassium reduced with and without sodium replacement.
evidence.uncertainty: Figure readings, not tabulated slopes. The pipette supplies the extracellular patch solution. Cell-attached recordings leave intracellular K activity unknown. The published power fit uses activity in the Na-substitution series. Cells takes concentrations.
evidence.assessment: Inward unitary slope fell from about 42 to 35 pS for 150→20 mM K without external Na, and to about 18.5 pS with 130 mM external Na. The concentration-based square-root prediction is 15.3 pS in either low-K solution.

evidence.locator: Figs. 1–2 and accompanying group slope estimates, open-cell-attached guinea-pig ventricular patches, Mg-free cytoplasm.
evidence.context: Native guinea-pig ventricular inward rectifier, internally Mg-free, with largely sugar-substituted low external K.
evidence.uncertainty: The two rows at 150 mM internal K compare quasi-linear single-channel slopes with sugar substitution outside. Molecular identity was unresolved. The third row changes the inside concentration.
evidence.assessment: Lowering external K from 150 to 30 mM gave 23.1 ± 1.2 pS against 14.2 pS predicted from the high-K anchor of 31.7 ± 1.7 pS. The group slopes are mean ± SD.

biology.finding: Reversal moved toward positive voltages when external potassium rose in two preparations. The inward unitary conductance increased with potassium in both recombinant series, with different concentration dependence. In a separate sodium-poor comparison the low-K slopes exceed high-K-anchored square-root predictions in both preparations.

pairs.assumption: Inward Kir4.1 unitary slope conductance follows the square root of external potassium across preparations.
pairs.independence: Tada’s group recorded rat Kir4.1 in HEK293T. Edvinsson’s group recorded human Kir4.1 in cell-attached oocyte patches.
pairs.comparison: Tada fitted a concentration exponent of 0.51 at 15–153 mM (three patches per level). Edvinsson fitted saturation. Anchoring a square root at their 110 mM value of 23 pS gives 13.9 pS at 40 mM, against about 19 pS in Fig. 7C. Both series rise. The figure precision, species and solutions limit inference about the difference.

replay.assessment: Tada’s fitted exponent is close to 0.5. In Edvinsson’s preparation the anchored law gives 13.9 versus about 19 pS at 40 mM. The two Kir4.1 preparations differ. The separate Na-poor inward-rectifier comparison has different channel identities.

pairs.assumption: Raising external potassium shifts the reversal of Kir4.1 or a Kir-dominated Müller-cell current to more positive voltages.
pairs.independence: The recombinant rat-channel study and native frog retinal-glia study used separate preparations in different laboratories.
pairs.comparison: The recombinant crossing moved about +60 mV from 15 to 153 mM K. One frog Müller cell gave about +50 mV from 1 to 10 mM at fixed pipette spermine. The measurements support the reversal direction. Neither the representative native trace nor its block breakpoint determines a universal reversal slope.

replay.assessment: The native K zero gains about one thermal decade in both preparations, consistent with measured changes near +60 and +50 mV. The glial record gives one crossing per solution. Internal K cancels from the shift at fixed temperature.

pairs.assumption: In Na-poor external solutions, one high-K calibration and square-root concentration scaling predict the low-K inward unitary slope.
pairs.independence: Ishihara measured recombinant mouse Kir2.1 in L cells. Matsuda recorded separate native guinea-pig ventricular patches. The molecular subtype of the latter was unresolved.
pairs.comparison: For 150→20 mM K, recombinant inward slope retained about 35/42 = 83% without Na. For 150→30 mM K, the native Mg-free slope retained 23.1/31.7 = 73%. Nominal-concentration predictions are 37% and 45%. This compares slope measurements across preparations.

replay.assessment: Using nominal solution labels at matched inward drive, the high-K anchored native slope ratios are 0.365 and 0.447 versus about 0.83 and 0.729. Each experiment fits slopes over a voltage range. At 20 mM K, Ishihara’s Na-substituted value drops toward the square-root prediction. Molecular identity of the native ventricular current is unresolved. Using the Fig. 4 total K concentrations from Ishihara Table 2 gives 0.378 and 0.570 at 21.3 and 48.4 mM, relative to 149.1 mM. The matched-drive prediction for Matsuda remains 0.447.

claims.title: The eight-state sodium–anion carrier shares a cycle flux and saturates with external substrate
claims.statement: Each edge of a steady ring carries the same net flux. For the declared two-sodium, one-anion cycle, exact detailed balance gives the host’s thermodynamic turnover and stall. For an active population at fixed voltage, sodium and internal substrate, the increase in inward current over its zero-substrate limit has the form A x / (K + x) for positive A and K.
assumptions: The carrier is at steady state on the single eight-edge ring with positive microscopic rates. Its forward and backward directions each bind the two sodium ions and the anion in the declared order. One net positive charge enters per forward cycle.

Equality with the thermodynamic rate assumes equal products of the base rate constants and a net electrical coefficient of −1 in the forward direction. A separate theorem retains the constant and voltage residuals for populations admitted within the engine’s detailed-balance tolerance.

The current comparison requires positive capacity and availability. The saturation result holds at fixed temperature, voltage, availability, all other activities and rate parameters. External substrate changes only its one forward binding rate. The reference current at zero substrate is the boundary value of the mass-action expression. The observed current is the measured steady current after subtracting its substrate-free baseline.

numerical.result: The capacity repair passed the original controls and all four extreme/zero capacity cases on NumPy and compiled CPU. At 10⁻³⁰² fmol/s the net readouts both gave 7.09691 × 10⁻³⁰⁵ fmol/s and reverse readouts gave 2.67423 × 10⁻³⁰⁷ fmol/s. The previous 100-fold diagnostic error remains recorded at its tested revision.

pairs.assumption: Human SMCT1 substrate-induced current saturates as external propionate increases at −50 mV.
pairs.independence: Miyauchi’s and Paroder’s groups recorded their own oocytes expressing human SMCT1.
pairs.comparison: The published half-saturation concentrations were 127 ± 14 and 162 ± 26 µM. The dose responses independently support saturation and an affinity scale around 0.1–0.2 mM. The exact affinity, eight transition rates and sodium coupling ratio remain separate questions.

replay.assessment: Separate two-point fits give 130 and 140 µM. The saturating response matches direction and approximate scale on held-out doses in both reports. Transition rates and the sodium coupling count require different observables.

biology.observable: Baseline-subtracted steady current as external monocarboxylate concentration or clamped voltage changes. The dose series tests the functional form. A biological assignment for the individual transition rates and voltage coefficients remains open.
biology.unit: nA inward magnitude (propionate), µA signed current (lactate)
biology.finding: In an independent human SMCT oocyte series at −50 mV, the propionate half-saturation concentration was 128 ± 4 µM (SEM, n = 9). This pooled estimate constrains affinity. [Coady et al., Fig. 3A](https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.2004.063859)

evidence.locator: The data are the six filled symbols in the main propionate panel.
evidence.context: Human SLC5A8 in one representative Xenopus oocyte at −50 mV, 100 mM external sodium and pH 7.5. The inward current is measured relative to the substrate-free baseline.
evidence.uncertainty: The approximate graph-reading precision is ±5 nA. Per-point biological uncertainties and the measurement temperature are unspecified. The paper reports similar results from three additional oocytes.
evidence.assessment: Two calibration points gave K = 130 µM. At 250 µM the proven curve predicted 260 nA against 278 nA measured. At 2,500 µM it predicted 376 nA against 371 nA. The figure provides too little biological uncertainty for a population verdict.

evidence.locator: Subtract the substrate-free ibuprofen-sensitive trace from the 1 mM lactate trace at each negative voltage.
evidence.context: Human SMCT1 in a Xenopus oocyte, 96 mM external sodium, approximately 24 °C and pH 7.6.
excluded: Positive-voltage currents dominated by an anion leak
evidence.uncertainty: One representative experiment, approximate reading precision ±0.03 µA. Intracellular activities and kinetic parameters for this preparation are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: The inward current rose from about 0.68 to 1.40 µA in magnitude between −50 and −150 mV. Predicting that voltage dependence requires the transition kinetics.

evidence.locator: Filled symbols of the human propionate dose response at −50 mV.
evidence.context: Independent human SMCT oocyte series. The same two nominal calibration doses were used on this experiment’s current scale.
evidence.uncertainty: The caption gives n = 3 for the kinetic analysis. Pointwise biological errors and how the symbols aggregate the recordings are unspecified. Estimated figure precision is ±0.6 nA and about ±15 µM at low dose.
evidence.assessment: At nominal 200 µM, 22.6 nA was observed and 22.45 nA predicted. The two-point fit gave half-saturation of 140.2 µM and the paper reports 162 ± 26 µM. The original 250 µM residual remains untested in this independent series.

claims.title: Sodium coupling sets net charge and the stall voltage of an anion carrier
claims.statement: A forward cycle imports n sodium ions and one monovalent anion. The two source-side saturations and capacity scale the net rate. With n > 1 the carrier imports below its unique stall voltage. With n = 1 its rate is independent of voltage.
assumptions: Positive concentrations at N and P and a forward cycle from P to N. Both roles use the same standard state at their two ends. The engine admits n = 1, 2, 3 or 4. Capacity, availability and both saturations are positive in the active-stall theorem.

Equal-fraction external sodium and substrate changes assume fixed internal activities. Measured whole-cell voltage shifts yield the isolated shift ratio if both changes carry the same nonzero conductance weighting.

numerical.result: All 120 stages agreed with independent 60-digit free energies, saturation, rates and heat. The panel covered both orientations, all four sodium counts and twelve active stalls. The two-step tissue run gained exactly the lactate amount recorded as transported cycles and reported zero global charge error.

pairs.assumption: Each human SMCT1 cycle imports two Na⁺ per propionate.
pairs.independence: Gopal’s and Coady’s groups studied human SMCT1 in separate oocyte experiments. Coady is the source of the Cells two-sodium choice.
pairs.comparison: Gopal reported 2.7 ± 0.2 net positive charges per propionate. With monovalent propionate and fully coupled current that implies 3.7 ± 0.2 Na⁺ per substrate. Coady measured 2.3 ± 0.3 Na⁺ per propionate from paired shifts in zero-current voltage (n = 7, SEM). Uncoupled current and passive propionic-acid uptake affect the inference. The two assays give different estimates for this substrate.

replay.assessment: Current per labelled uptake and shifts in zero-current voltage imply different apparent sodium counts. A matched accounting of neutral entry and uncoupled current is missing.

biology.observable: Charge per lactate, particles per charge and the ratio of voltage shifts with external sodium and substrate halving in human SMCT1.

evidence.locator: Fig. 9B and accompanying human SLC5A8 results, p. 44530.
evidence.context: Human SMCT expressed in Xenopus oocytes. Integrated substrate-induced current and radiolabel uptake.
evidence.uncertainty: The ± is the authors' reported SE. The human series is distinct from the mouse series and from Fig. 9A lactate.
evidence.assessment: Human SMCT1 gave 2.7 ± 0.2 net charges per propionate. With a monovalent anion and entirely coupled current, the implied sodium count is 3.7 ± 0.2.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 compares lactate uptake with current, and Fig. 2 compares volume with current. Fig. 4 uses both 96 to 48 mM and 48 to 24 mM sodium steps, each paired with substrate halving.
evidence.context: Human SMCT1 in Xenopus oocytes. The Cells declaration cites this study for the two-sodium coupling.
evaluation: Lactate and propionate zero-current shift ratios
evidence.uncertainty: The reported charge uncertainty was ±0.07 across five batch slopes. The volume/current and shift ratios are reported as mean ± SE.
evidence.assessment: The two-sodium carrier also predicted 3 osmolytes per charge versus 3.1 ± 0.1 measured. It predicted a shift ratio of 2 for both sodium halvings. The experimental means were 2.2 ± 0.2 for lactate and 2.3 ± 0.3 for propionate. Absolute stall and Hill kinetics remain open.

evidence.locator: Human series, square symbols. The x axis is integrated charge and the y axis is radiolactate uptake.
evidence.context: An independent laboratory measured human SMCT in Xenopus oocytes. The coupling was fixed from the Coady study.
fit: Coupling n = 2 from Coady et al.
evaluation: Four distinguishable human lactate uptake/current pairs
evidence.uncertainty: Approximate figure readings rounded to 5 pmol. Individual experimental uncertainties are unavailable.
evidence.assessment: Measured net charge exceeded the prediction at all four human points by approximately 65–85 pmol. At 370 pmol lactate, Cells predicted 370 pmol net charge and the figure gives about 450 pmol.

claims.title: Potassium–anion cotransport follows the concentration products in a closed pair
claims.statement: The active 1:1 route moves outward when the inside concentration product is larger, stalls at equality and dissipates nonnegative heat. Equal amounts of the two ions move together. With equal fixed volumes, the exact trajectory approaches equilibrium monotonically. An explicit ARS(2,2,2) step can move in the opposite direction if it is too large for the closed pair.
assumptions: Potassium has valence +1 and its partner −1. Concentrations and temperature are positive. The rate scale is capacity times availability times the exponential volume factor. Strict direction and stall require a positive scale.

The closed-pair trajectory assumes one route, equal fixed finite volumes, constant availability and no other transfers. The explicit stage calculation uses the ARS(2,2,2) order condition. All formal operations are in real arithmetic.

numerical.result: After the product-ratio fix, both extreme concentration cases gave finite affinity and heat matching the independent references. At 2⁻⁵¹⁰ mM outside they were 1,836,599.47 J/mol and 4,701.69 pJ/s. All 27 ordinary controls passed. With fixed and moving water, the original 10 ms step was refused and the 32- and 64-step refinements passed. The previous failed cases remain in the earlier checkpoints.

biology.observable: External cation concentration at reversal normalized by internal potassium, plotted against the inside/outside chloride ratio.
biology.finding: Rabbit red cells gave an outward K:Cl flux ratio of 1.12 ± 0.26 (SD, five preparations), consistent with the model’s 1:1 stoichiometry. The investigators measured rubidium as a potassium tracer and calibrated its relative flux. [Jennings and Adame, Fig. 5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11502559/)

pairs.assumption: Changing external potassium can reverse the direction of K–Cl cotransport.
pairs.independence: Separate groups studied sheep erythrocytes and rat neurons. The first measured K⁺ efflux and Rb⁺ influx. The second inferred transport direction from the blocker-sensitive electrical response.
pairs.comparison: Lauf and Adragna located net-flux zeros in sheep red cells using external Rb⁺ as the K⁺ surrogate. In rat dendrites at 4.5 mM pipette anion, blocking transport shifted GABA reversal by +7.0 ± 0.9 mV at 2 mM external K⁺ and −5.0 ± 0.7 mV at 10 mM (SEM). The change of sign supports reversal. The neuronal voltage assay does not locate a flux zero or test a unit activity-product ratio.

replay.assessment: The native 1:1 product rule reverses signed flux and is consistent with the sheep null measurements. The dendritic readout is a blocker-induced GABA voltage change. A local free chloride gradient and conversion to a transport rate are missing.

pairs.assumption: Equality of the nominal intracellular and extracellular K–Cl concentration products locates zero flux in swollen sheep erythrocytes across protocols.
pairs.independence: The later paper revisits the earlier same-laboratory result, with Lauf on both papers and a different protocol. These reports document sensitivity to the preparation. A second group’s direct measurement of the null remains open.
pairs.comparison: The 1991 swelling experiment still had outward net K⁺ flux at equal products and approached zero near an outside/inside ratio of 2. In the later pH- and volume-clamped experiments, normalized reversal had slopes of 1.12 and 1.08 for normal and low internal Mg²⁺ (ideal 1). They report different apparent nulls. Activities and protocol differences preclude transferring the earlier value to the clamped preparation.

replay.assessment: The swelling and clamped protocols give different apparent nulls and share a research group. Activities and the time-dependent volume are needed for matched native nulls.

pairs.assumption: The red-cell K–Cl cotransporter carries approximately one potassium ion per chloride ion.
pairs.comparison: In sheep red cells, normalized external Rb⁺ at the flux null had slopes of 1.12 and 1.08 against the chloride ratio (normal and low Mg²⁺, no slope errors). In rabbit red cells, a direct outward K:Cl flux ratio was 1.12 ± 0.26 (SD, five experiments). These readouts independently support approximately 1:1 coupling. Only the sheep series located the null.
pairs.independence: Lauf and Adragna inferred stoichiometry from flux-reversal shifts. Jennings and Adame measured ion efflux in separate rabbit preparations.

replay.assessment: The native postings are one K and one Cl per cycle. This is compatible with the rabbit direct efflux ratio and the near-unit slope of the sheep null series. Only the latter is a test at zero net flux.

pairs.assumption: Chloride contributes to the direction of volume-sensitive erythrocyte K–Cl cotransport.
pairs.independence: The Lauf and Brugnara groups independently measured sheep and human erythrocytes. The sheep assay used Rb as a K surrogate.
pairs.comparison: Sheep net-flux zeros shifted with the chloride ratio, with fitted slopes 1.12 and 1.08 in two magnesium conditions. In human cells an outward Cl gradient drove K outward against its own gradient at fixed membrane potential.

replay.assessment: The native product law permits this direction. The human finding supplies no matched measurement of the nominal sheep concentration product at zero flux. Its exact threshold remains open.

evidence.locator: Fig. 6B and adjoining low-pipette-anion results.
evidence.context: Dendrites of cultured rat midbrain neurons. The furosemide-induced shift in GABA-current reversal was measured at two external K⁺ concentrations.
evidence.uncertainty: Values are mean ± SEM. Pipette permeant anion and local free chloride activity are distinct. Transport direction is inferred from the blocker-sensitive voltage shift.
evidence.assessment: The opposite dendritic voltage responses support a reversal in K–Cl transport direction as external K⁺ rises. No absolute K–Cl flux or independently measured product of activities at zero transport is available.

evidence.locator: Abstract and results on net potassium efflux at equal and reversed concentration products.
evidence.context: Hyposmotically swollen low-K sheep red cells. Net K flux was compared across concentrations and temperatures.
evidence.uncertainty: Approximate concentration-product ratio reported by the authors. The exact zero and an uncertainty were not reported for this summary.
evidence.assessment: Net efflux persisted at equal concentration products and approached zero near twice the internal product. Lauf’s later pH- and volume-clamped study tested this discrepancy with a different protocol.

evidence.locator: Fig. 5 and accompanying K:Cl outward-flux ratio results.
evidence.context: N-ethylmaleimide-stimulated rabbit erythrocytes. The sulfate bath and anion-exchanger inhibition allowed comparison of K and Cl efflux.
evidence.uncertainty: Mean ± SD over five experiments. The two ionic fluxes define a stoichiometric ratio away from the null.
evidence.assessment: The independently measured outward K:Cl flux ratio of 1.12 ± 0.26 is compatible with 1:1 coupling in this preparation. Its zero-flux concentration product was not measured.

evidence.locator: Figures 5–7 estimate the reversal point from zero net flux. Figure 8 fits normalized reversal against the chloride ratio.
evidence.context: Low-potassium sheep red cells with pH and volume clamped. The assay compared outward K and inward Rb flux after chloride-minus-nitrate subtraction.
evidence.uncertainty: Eight points contributed to the normal-magnesium fit and ten to the low-magnesium fit. The paper gives correlations of 0.912 and 0.976. It gives no uncertainty for either slope.
evidence.assessment: The ideal product rule predicts a slope of 1. The measured slopes were 1.12 at normal magnesium and 1.08 at low magnesium. Rubidium substitutes for external potassium. The volume dependence of net flux remains open.

evidence.locator: Net K flux under opposed gradients, pp. C994–C1003.
evidence.context: Volume-sensitive transport in human red cells. Permeant substitute anions stabilized membrane potential while anion exchange was inhibited.
evidence.uncertainty: The direction is reported directly. A matched sweep of internal and external activities through a measured zero is unavailable here.
evidence.assessment: An outward chloride gradient drove net K efflux against the K gradient. This constrains the direction under combined ion gradients.

claims.title: Water potential sets flow, heat and osmometric equilibrium
claims.statement: Water moves down the hydrostatic-minus-osmotic pressure difference. At frozen solute amounts this potential is the volume derivative of free energy after unit conversion. Dissipated heat is nonnegative. An outward potassium–anion cycle increases the outward water drive by moving two osmoles across the membrane.
assumptions: All volumes and temperature are positive. Osmoles are ideal, elastic pressure is linear in volume, and mobility and stiffness are nonnegative. Each held bath has fixed pressure and concentrations.

The Heun direction result applies to one finite edge at frozen amounts. Both positive predictor volumes are at least one quarter of their respective start volumes, and the full-step mobility times the sum of the initial pressure slopes is at most 0.05.

The equilibrium comparisons use positive mobility. The vesicle fit uses a common effective modulus across two small swelling conditions. The ideal red-cell comparison uses aqueous volume and a separate inactive-volume estimate for each preparation.

numerical.result: Five accepted CPU float64 runs tested water alone and water coupled to potassium–anion transport. Halving the step in two coupled worlds reduced the errors in both transfers and both heats by factors of 4.00–4.11 against an independent two-extent calculation. Separate oversized water and cotransport inputs triggered their respective step bounds.

pairs.assumption: A hyperosmotic external bath draws water out of protein-free phospholipid vesicles.
pairs.independence: Mathai’s and Frallicciardi’s groups performed separate stopped-flow experiments. Only the latter paper’s experimental panels are used.
pairs.comparison: Both experiments detected shrinkage by dye quenching. Their fitted DOPC/POPC water permeabilities were 15.8/13.0 at 30 °C and 16.0/12.0 at 20 °C, in 10⁻³ cm/s. Flow direction is the shared prediction. Lipid ordering constrains mobility inputs and heat was unmeasured.

replay.assessment: The native water flux points outward when external osmotic pressure increases at equal hydrostatic pressure. Both stopped-flow traces shrink. Lipid-specific mobility is an input. A quantitative trace also requires vesicle sizes and fluorescence-to-volume calibration.

biology.observable: Equilibrium swelling in vesicles and red cells, water flow after pressure steps in a Chara internode, and the water change accompanying net solute movement in trout red cells. A pathway-specific rate for K–anion cotransport during swelling remains open.
biology.unit: % swelling, fL cell volume, nL/s inward flow, g water per g dry cell solids

evidence.citation: Mathai et al. (2008), Fig. 1A and Table I
evidence.locator: Fig. 1A, Table I and water-permeability methods.
evidence.context: Protein-free vesicles under a 50% increase in external osmotic pressure, 30 °C. Entrapped dye self-quenching reported volume loss.
evidence.uncertainty: 8–12 traces averaged for a fluorescence curve. The Table I ± convention is unspecified here.
evidence.assessment: The hyperosmotic bath induced water efflux. DOPC and POPC water permeability were 15.8 ± 0.58 and 13.0 ± 0.44 in units of 10⁻³ cm/s at 30 °C.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1A and experimental panels 3A and 4A.
evidence.context: Lipid vesicles under an external osmotic upshift, 20 °C. Only stopped-flow fluorescence data are used.
evidence.uncertainty: Figures report SEM. Methods propagate uncertainty in vesicle size distributions. Individual repeated size determinations do not establish independent preparations.
evidence.assessment: The hyperosmotic stopped-flow experiment detected shrinkage. DOPC and POPC water permeability were 16.0 ± 1.7 and 12.0 ± 1.4 in units of 10⁻³ cm/s at 20 °C.

evidence.locator: Figure 2B and the adjacent results give the equilibrium volume increments after single-vesicle transfers.
evidence.context: DOPC vesicles at 25 ± 1 °C contained 98 mM sucrose and were transferred into glucose solutions.
evidence.uncertainty: The reported ±0.1 percentage point has unspecified statistic. The two concentration steps are nominal.
evidence.assessment: A stiffness fitted to 1.7% swelling predicted 2.57% on the second bath against 2.6 ± 0.1% measured.

evidence.locator: Table II, 126 mOsm/L ghost series, and Table I, Coulter measurements of intact cells.
evidence.context: Sealed human red-cell ghosts were sized at 37 °C. Temperature for intact-cell sizing is unspecified. Each calibration uses the study's separate estimate of inactive volume.
evidence.uncertainty: The volume spreads are reported SDs. The calibration volume, inactive volume and bath osmolarity contribute additional uncertainty to predictions.
evidence.assessment: At 184 mOsm/L the ideal model predicted 111.4 fL for ghosts (109.0 ± 1.0 measured) and 122.6 fL for intact cells (111.5 ± 1.2 measured).

evidence.locator: Figure 2A gives the first 40 s slopes of two opposite pressure clamps on cell 12.
evidence.context: A Chara corallina internode in artificial pond water at 23 ± 2 °C re-equilibrated between the two pressure steps.
evidence.uncertainty: Individual slope uncertainties are unavailable. The second resting turgor was 0.060 bar lower.
evidence.assessment: One measured pressure step predicted reversed water flow of 4.82 nL/s outward on the second step. The measured flow was 5.3 nL/s outward.

evidence.locator: Figure 1 and Table 1 give the 60-minute water and solute changes after initial hypotonic swelling.
evidence.context: Rainbow-trout red cells were held at 215 mOsm/kg with ouabain. Each condition measured changes in cellular water, sodium, potassium, chloride and taurine.
excluded: Choline bath, total osmole change unavailable
evidence.uncertainty: The paper reports SEM. The water prediction uses the measured osmole total. Covariance with measured water is unavailable.
evidence.assessment: Measured osmole changes imply water changes of −0.375 and +0.078 g/g in two baths, against −0.37 and +0.06 measured. Multiple transport pathways contribute.

claims.title: Regional inventory changes by net boundary transfer across a split step
claims.statement: A reaction–transport–reaction step changes a region’s weighted inventory by exactly its signed boundary inflow. The total over a closed graph is conserved.
assumptions: Node identities and the region stay fixed. Every local reaction inside the region balances the inventory. Each transport edge debits and credits its endpoints.

numerical.result: In a 50 ms CPU step, the change in A + B across four compartments agreed with boundary inflow within 1.07 × 10⁻¹⁹ fmol. Reversing a crossing face failed the regional check while the whole chain still balanced.

biology.observable: Change in the amount of a named chemical group inside a defined tissue region and its net passage across that boundary over the same interval.
biology.finding: A perfused rat liver study followed labeled carbon in tissue, perfusate, bile and CO₂. Reconstructing the balance requires matched time intervals, sample volumes and coverage of the other tissue pools. [Fausto, Fig. 1](https://doi.org/10.1042/bj1290811)

claims.title: Membrane voltage in kidney epithelial cells under condition C3
claims.statement: In the fixed Na/K substitution series, two passive reversal voltages determine the higher-potassium C3 prediction. The assigned figure-reading intervals bound the prediction, its change from the shared C1 baseline and the signed error.
assumptions: The reference calculation assumes fixed intracellular ion concentrations and relative permeabilities across conditions, at zero applied current and 25 °C. It omits pump and intercellular currents.
External Na plus K and external Cl stay fixed. The two fitting doses are distinct. The exact C3 extrapolation has weight two, with a positive log argument throughout the assigned reading box.

numerical.result: The fixed reference predicted −14.59 mV. All 81 sampled fit-reading pairs respected the proved corner bounds and twelve 60-digit crosschecks agreed within 7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ mV. On three synthetic membranes with rising, flat and falling responses, the third-dose predictions agreed with the independent engine reversal within 2.05 × 10⁻¹⁴ mV.

biology.observable: Whole-cell resting membrane voltage after application of extracellular solution C3.

evidence.locator: Figure 2A–B gives the solution series. The C3 measurement is an approximate mean read from the patch-clamp results in Figure 3C.
evidence.context: RPTEC/TERT1 renal proximal tubule epithelial cells, whole-cell patch recording at zero applied current and 25 °C. C3 reports 20 cells across three experiments.
evidence.uncertainty: The ±2 mV bound describes the curator’s figure reading. The numerical standard error of the mean and the dependence between condition summaries are unknown.
evidence.assessment: The retrospective C3 prediction was 3.41 mV above the figure reading. The closeout records a descriptive result. Biological acceptance remains unresolved because experimental uncertainty and the recording boundary are insufficiently characterized.

claims.title: Shell entry and exit depend on conductance and the gate’s own forms
claims.statement: At fixed activities and standard density, the area–permeability product fixes both rate prefactors. Changing other wall counts leaves the gate factor unchanged. The common gate preserves the ratio of the two directional activities when the reverse rate is positive.
assumptions: The declared area and lumen volume are fixed. Forward and reverse comparisons use their respective activities and the same gate counts on the pair’s common state.
The gate factor is a count-weighted mean over its declared forms. An absent gate has factor one.

numerical.result: Two existing engine tests passed. Doubling area while halving permeability preserved both rates to rounding. Doubling permeability alone doubled both rates. Changes to nongate inventory left rates and lumen volume identical. Both run modes recorded the shell probe.

biology.observable: Bidirectional flux at measured shell area and permeability, with the gate-form ratio held fixed while nongate site counts vary.

claims.title: A sealed shell excludes a ligand when its bound forms stay on one face
claims.statement: If every event conserves a ligand moiety and every possible transfer preserves its face, an initially ligand-free interior stays free through any finite event history. A ligand in the final free lumen has an initially occupied origin connected by transfers. Binding another ligand can carry the first one across a wall reaction.
assumptions: Places include free pools and all wall forms. A nonnegative integer weight gives each place’s number of copies of the selected moiety per molecule. Every directed event consumes available molecules and balances their weighted counts. Include both directions of reversible reactions.

Each consumed place with positive moiety weight connects to every produced place carrying that moiety in the same event. Each such connection must preserve its face. This sufficient condition can conservatively connect distinct copies when a reaction carries several.
Every inner-accessible place, including bound complexes, starts with zero copies of the selected moiety. The free lumen place has positive weight. Other ligands may already be present inside.

numerical.result: The original candidate 61d823be admitted the four-event carrier. After the face rule began following ligand already on a site through other binding events, the unchanged reproducer passed on d19b10c2 and cf5ddcff. Both refused the path through A, C and D and admitted the sealed control with Y binding removed. The owner’s regression also passed on cf5ddcff.

biology.observable: Lumen tracer count over time in a closed shell with face-selective binding, with the initially free and wall-bound tracer inventories measured.

claims.title: Dissipated free energy as tracer refills a washed pool
claims.statement: Between washes the free energy of the two mean tracer counts is nonincreasing, including at an empty starting place. Its drop is the deterministic continuous interval heat. Replacing an empty place’s initial term by its one-molecule value shifts the heat by (μ° − ln X − 1) kBT when both final counts are positive.
assumptions: Two well-mixed compartments of fixed positive volumes exchange a single passive tracer during the interval. Temperature, standard potentials and the shell conductance are fixed. The surviving mean counts are nonnegative and their sum is conserved. Unchanged wall terms cancel in the difference.

The free energy of a place in kBT is n(μ° − ln X) + n ln n − n, with μ° in RT units, X = N_A V c₀ in molecules and the continuous value zero at n = 0. Positive entry and exit rates obey ln k_in − ln k_out = (μ°outside − ln Xoutside) − (μ°inside − ln Xinside). A completely impermeable shell has both rates zero.
The interval runs from just after the preceding wash to just before the following wash, or to the observation horizon. Each wash carries its own work, sink and mixing entries.

numerical.result: On development build 43763a36, all three synthetic intervals agreed within 6.60 × 10⁻⁸ kBT. After full replacement the engine booked 38.34719503 kBT against 38.34719500 predicted. The whole-term substitution gave 24.33882673 kBT. It also changed the empty-lumen interval and had zero effect on the interval with two occupied places. This comparison uses invented inputs. D373 records the independent FR-47 qualification and the separate schedule check. [Qualification decision](https://github.com/Eidosoma/Cells/blob/9b6191bdf0800d70dcae81107378401ab3c8b474/docs/DECISIONS.md#L12337-L12362)

biology.observable: Free energy dissipated as tracer returns to a freshly washed finite exterior, measured by reversible work or inferred from independent chemical-potential differences over the transfer.

claims.title: Tracer returns to a finite exterior pool after a wash
claims.statement: A full tracer-free wash leaves the retained lumen mean L and sets the exterior count to zero. With constant per-molecule rates k_in into the lumen and k_out back out, the exterior mean at elapsed time t is L k_out (1 − exp(−s t))/s, where s = k_in + k_out > 0. Its right derivative at the wash is k_out L. A later withdrawal of fraction f on the sampler’s word grid removes f times that recovered mean.
assumptions: A finite set of tracers exchanges between two well-mixed compartments of fixed positive volume. Each tracer obeys the two-state forward equation between washes. Molecules removed by a wash stay absent. The interval has constant rates and conserves the surviving tracer.

The physical rates per second are k_in = P A / V_out and k_out = P A exp(Δ) / V_in, with volumes in m³, permeability P in m/s, area A in m² and Δ = (μ°lumen − μ°solution)/RT. A fixed gate can multiply both rates by the same factor.

A complete replacement exchanges the exterior for tracer-free medium. At the next fractional withdrawal, each exterior molecule has the declared removal probability, independently, under the sampler’s equal-weight word law. The fraction is exactly representable on its grid.

numerical.result: On cf5ddcff replacement removed five exterior tracers and left seven in the lumen. The eight-state host rate matrix gave exterior means of 1.3607043414 at 0.75 s and 2.8910229384 at 2 s. The native half-withdrawal averaged 1.4455114692 removed. All agreed within 10⁻¹² molecules. On the separate deterministic development build 43763a36, all six compartment reads and both removed amounts met a 0.00024-molecule tolerance on an invented 240-tracer shell. FR-47 subsequently passed its registered qualification. [D373](https://github.com/Eidosoma/Cells/blob/9b6191bdf0800d70dcae81107378401ab3c8b474/docs/DECISIONS.md#L12337-L12362)

biology.observable: Exterior tracer recovered after a full wash, paired with retained lumen tracer and subsequent exterior sampling, at measured compartment volumes and independently calibrated exchange rates.

evidence.locator: Figure 2 and the buffer-control release half-time on page 179.
evidence.context: Single-bilayer DPPC vesicles, carboxyfluorescein loaded at 20 mM, exterior dye removed by chromatography, pH 7.4, 37 °C.

claims.title: The lumen tracer count has a binomial equilibrium in a prescribed shell
claims.statement: Let Δ be the lumen standard potential minus the solution standard potential, both in units of RT. With N molecules and equal volumes, the binomial distribution with lumen probability p = 1/(1 + exp Δ) is normalized and satisfies detailed balance at every adjacent count. It is stationary in continuous time. The mean lumen count is Np. For N > 0 the ratio of mean inside to mean outside concentration is exp(−Δ).
assumptions: A single conserved neutral tracer moves between a finite solution pool and a prescribed lumen of the same fixed positive volume. The only events changing its counts are single-molecule crossings. Both places use the same temperature and standard concentration.

At lumen count k the total entry rate is h(N−k). From k+1 the exit rate back to k is h(k+1) exp Δ. The common per-molecule rate h comes from permeability, area, volume and a fixed wall gate. A positive h permits crossings in both directions.
The expectation is over the count at equilibrium in physical time. Each count has the probability assigned by the normalized distribution, including the endpoints at zero and N.

numerical.result: The frozen development engine at 61d823be matched the reference binomial probabilities within 10⁻¹² for 12 tracers at Δ = ln 2, equal potentials and the undeclared default. Its CPU test detected the incorrect offset interpretation and verified ledger closure from both extreme initial distributions.

biology.observable: Equilibrium counts of one conserved neutral tracer inside and outside an equal-volume compartment pair, with an independently determined transfer free energy at the same temperature.

claims.title: Replacing occupied sites accounts for departing and arriving bound ligand
claims.statement: For each due population the newcomer carries its template occupancy times its capacity. Site-bound ligand after the event plus departures equals site-bound ligand before the event plus arrivals. Free ligand common to the two sides cancels.
assumptions: The identity isolates the site operator at the event. The host accounts separately for changes to free pools, reactions and binding between rows.
Each due population has an admitted template and a fixed site capacity. Other populations retain their bound amount.

numerical.result: In the compiled world with occupied sites and ongoing conversion, maximum ligand and product balance residuals were at most 10⁻¹⁵ fmol. Dropping departing ligand from the balance produced the expected deficit. The site-readout regression also read the newcomer’s occupancy after reset. These cargo and occupancy controls passed on 68ab12e7. At the replacement time the exported reaction rate mixed the departing substrate and incoming multiplier. D264 holds that row from scoring.

biology.observable: Cross-event inventories of free and occupant-bound ligand with independently measured departing and arriving cargo.

claims.title: A wash at the same ion concentration must collect and supply equal amounts
claims.statement: For an unchanged ion in a well of positive volume, replacing a fraction of liquid with solution at the well’s concentration preserves the ion inventory. The collected amount equals the supplied amount at every fraction in exact arithmetic. The engine specifies an exact equality for the corresponding cumulative counters.
assumptions: Collection and refill use the same fraction, volume, ion and concentration. Both counters start from equal values. The compiled fixture holds the well at fixed volume without any other ion transfer.

numerical.result: On the repaired compiled host, three half washes and three 3/7 washes kept Na, K and Cl inventories fixed. Collected and supplied counters agreed exactly at every saved row and both runs completed. At 68ab12e7 the 3/7 schedule left a chloride residual of −2.98 × 10⁻⁸ fmol and the outside-material ledger refused it.

biology.observable: Ion amounts in paired samples and refills at a matched electrolyte concentration and exchanged volume.

claims.title: A partial wash dilutes free tracer and preserves its inventory
claims.statement: For a finite well of fixed volume V, a wash of fraction f changes free amount n to (1 − f)n + f V c_buffer. Adding sampled material and subtracting supplied material recovers the original total, including bound ligand retained through the event. Repeating k equal washes multiplies the initial excess above the buffer level by (1 − f)ᵏ. For each exchanged neutral species, ideal mixing heat is nonnegative and a whole wash releases zero mixing heat.
assumptions: The liquid is well mixed. Between the washes used in the repeated-wash formula there is no binding, release, synthesis or transport. The landed tissue wash refuses a gene export into the washed node and outside degradation there. A different node remains eligible when its other admission conditions hold.

The Lean positivity result assumes 0 < f ≤ 1 and strictly positive free and buffer amounts. Float64 whole-wash storage also requires sufficient resolution at the host’s amount anchor. Version 1 exchanges ions at their own concentration.
For the heat, the well is ideal and isothermal with positive volume and concentrations and a nonnegative thermal energy scale.

numerical.result: Four compiled tracer schedules retained ions and site fields. The maximum tracer material discrepancy was 7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ fmol. Whole-wash runs reached 2⁻⁵⁰ of the initial amount and reproduced the documented refusal at 2⁻⁶⁰. The repaired counter check completed at fractions 1/2 and 3/7 with exact agreement for each unchanged ion. On b06158e8 and again after FR-49 landed at cd3b7b09, all 35 wash tests passed, including named same-node gene-route refusals and a separate-node admission.

biology.observable: Free tracer after successive known-fraction washes, together with independently measured ligand retained on the surface.

evidence.citation: Vloemans et al., Lab on a Chip (2024)
evidence.locator: Fig. 4A–B, printed mean concentrations
evidence.context: Free fluorescein in PBS, successive 10 µL plugs. For the numerical row, use the measured 1.712 µg/mL starting concentration and three 80% exchanges with blank buffer.
evidence.uncertainty: At least three replicates per point, with one SD drawn graphically. The comparison uses rounded printed means. The study notes wall adsorption and a limited instrument range.
evidence.assessment: The first two 80% washes measured 0.332 and 0.067 µg/mL against 0.3424 and 0.06848. The third mean was 46% above ideal dilution. The experiments address freely dissolved dye. Instantaneous bound-site retention in a biological well remains open.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1i, printed bar labels.
evidence.context: Well-to-well fluorescein carryover read in the channel 30 s after a change of well.
evidence.uncertainty: The last bar follows four wash wells. Each plotted residual already includes the fill delay.
evidence.assessment: Carryover was 0.23%, 0.07% and 0.02% after 0, 1 and 4 wash wells.

evidence.locator: Methods and Supplementary Fig. S-6A, also reproduced as Li’s dissertation Fig. 2.7A.
evidence.context: A fluorescein-filled reservoir was rinsed with buffer. Drained liquid was collected per outlet and read by fluorometry.
evidence.uncertainty: Panel A gives no replicate count or definition of the error bars. The volume SD in panel B belongs to a separate experiment.
evidence.assessment: The authors report under 1% after rinse 2. Rinse 5 is roughly 0.1% on the log inset, a reading of collected effluent.

pairs.assumption: Repeated buffer washes lower the signal from a preceding dye exposure in fluid collected or delivered by microfluidic devices.
pairs.independence: The Lagoy and Li groups built independent delivery systems. Li’s dissertation reprints the journal figure.
pairs.comparison: Lagoy measured 0.23%, 0.07% and 0.02% at 0, 1 and 4 wash wells. Li found <1% in fluid from the second rinse, with roughly 0.1% at the fifth rinse in the log inset.

replay.assessment: A compiled finite-pool wash gives monotone dilution. The first device measured channel signal after a fill delay and the second measured drained liquid. The data do not supply the same retained-pool fraction or a common fifth-rinse error.
